title: App deployment and management with Intune
summary: Learn how Microsoft Intune delivers and manages applications across Windows devices, from packaging Win32 apps to assigning them as Required or Available and troubleshooting why an install failed.
objectives: Identify the main app types Intune can deploy: Win32, line-of-business, Microsoft Store, web link, and Microsoft 365 apps
Package a Win32 application into the .intunewin format using the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool
Choose between Required, Available, and Uninstall assignment intents and explain each
Decide when to assign apps to user groups versus device groups
Explain how detection rules and the Company Portal report install status
Troubleshoot a common reason an assigned app failed to install

quiz.q: Which tool packages a Win32 application into the .intunewin file Intune needs?
quiz.why: The Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool (IntuneWinAppUtil.exe) wraps source files and the installer into a single .intunewin package for upload.

quiz.q: A user wants an optional app they can install on demand from the Company Portal. Which assignment intent fits?
quiz.why: Available makes the app optional and visible in the Company Portal so the user can choose to install it; Required force-installs without user action.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a detection rule on a Win32 app?
options: To decide which group receives the app
To tell Intune whether the app is already installed
To schedule a reboot after install
quiz.why: Detection rules (file, registry, MSI code, or script) let Intune determine current install state so it knows whether to install, skip, or report success.

quiz.q: You must guarantee a security agent is installed on every laptop regardless of who logs in. What should you do?
options: Assign it as Available to a user group
Assign it as Required to a device group
Publish it as a web link
quiz.why: Required assignment to a device group force-installs on the device itself, so it applies no matter which user signs in.

quiz.q: Where in the Intune admin center do you upload and assign applications, and what app type is used to deploy custom EXE-based installers?
quiz.answer: Go to the Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com) > Apps, then add the app; custom EXE or script-based installers are deployed as Win32 apps using a .intunewin package.
quiz.why: Apps is the dedicated workload for adding and assigning software, and Win32 app type handles EXE/MSI installers wrapped with the Content Prep Tool.

quiz.q: An app assigned as Required shows 'Failed' for several devices. Name two things you would check first.
quiz.answer: Check the detection rule (it may not correctly match the installed app) and verify the install command line, dependencies, and that the device is online and checked in; the Company Portal and device install status report give the error code.
quiz.why: Most Required-install failures trace to a wrong detection rule, a bad command line or missing dependency, or a device that has not yet synced; the status reports and error codes pinpoint which.

resources.label: Win32 app management in Microsoft Intune

body_markdown:
## Why app delivery matters

A huge slice of Tier 1 and Tier 2 work is getting the right software onto the right machine. With **Microsoft Intune** you stop walking USB sticks to desks and instead push apps from the cloud to enrolled Windows devices. Intune downloads the package, runs the installer silently, checks whether it worked, and reports status back to the admin center. Understanding this pipeline lets you move from "it won't install" tickets to confidently diagnosing the cause.

## App types in Intune

Intune supports several app types, each suited to a different source:

- **Win32 app** — your custom EXE, MSI, or script installers, packaged into a **.intunewin** file. This is the workhorse for in-house and third-party software.
- **Line-of-business (LOB) app** — a single MSI you upload directly, simpler but less flexible than Win32.
- **Microsoft Store app** — apps pulled from the new Microsoft Store integration; Intune handles updates automatically.
- **Web link** — a shortcut to a web app that appears in the Company Portal.
- **Microsoft 365 Apps** — a guided way to deploy Office (Word, Excel, Outlook) with channel and language options.

## Packaging a Win32 app

Win32 apps must be wrapped first. The **Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool** (`IntuneWinAppUtil.exe`) takes your source folder and setup file and produces one encrypted `.intunewin` package.

```powershell
IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c C:\Source -s setup.exe -o C:\Output
```

You then upload that `.intunewin`, specify the silent **install and uninstall commands**, and define a **detection rule** so Intune knows when the app is present.

## Assigning apps

Adding an app does nothing until you assign it. There are three intents:

- **Required** — Intune force-installs the app automatically.
- **Available for enrolled devices** — the app appears in the **Company Portal** for users to install on demand.
- **Uninstall** — Intune removes the app from targeted devices.

You assign to **Microsoft Entra groups**. A key decision is **user groups versus device groups**: assign to a *user* group when the app should follow the person (Available apps usually target users); assign to a *device* group when the software must be on the machine no matter who logs in, such as a security agent.

```text
Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com)
  > Apps > Windows > + Add
  > pick app type > upload package and set install/detect rules
  > Assignments > add group under Required / Available / Uninstall
```

## How status is reported

The **Company Portal** app is the user-facing storefront for Available apps and shows install progress. On the admin side, each app's **Device install status** and **User install status** pages report Installed, Failed, or Not applicable, along with an error code. The **detection rule** is what decides "Installed," so a mismatched rule is a frequent cause of phantom failures.

## Troubleshooting failures

When an app shows **Failed**, work through the basics: confirm the device has synced (it must check in to receive the assignment), verify the **install command line** is correct and silent, check for missing **dependencies**, and re-examine the **detection rule** to be sure it matches what the installer actually drops. Error codes from the status pages map to specific failures.

## Your task

In a test tenant, package a small free tool (for example, 7-Zip) into a `.intunewin` file with the Content Prep Tool, upload it as a Win32 app, set a detection rule, assign it as **Available** to a test user group, and confirm it appears in the Company Portal. Then add a second assignment as **Required** to a device group and verify the install status reports correctly.

slides.title: App deployment and management with Intune
slides.sub: Month 5 - Modern Endpoint Management with AI (MD-102)  |  Lesson 4
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Four of Month Five. Today we move into one of the most common parts of helpdesk work: getting software onto devices. Instead of carrying installers around on a USB stick, we'll use Microsoft Intune to push apps from the cloud, watch them install, and report back. By the end you'll understand the app types, how to package and assign software, and how to figure out why an install failed.

slides.title: Why deliver apps from the cloud?
bullets: Intune downloads, installs, and reports app status remotely.
No more walking USB sticks to every desk.
Moves you from guessing to diagnosing install issues.
Works on enrolled Windows devices managed by Intune.
slides.narration: Let's start with the big picture. A large share of Tier One and Tier Two tickets are simply about getting the right software onto the right machine. With Intune, you push apps from the cloud to enrolled devices. Intune downloads the package, runs the installer silently, checks whether it worked, and reports the status back to the admin center. Understanding that pipeline is what lets you stop guessing and start diagnosing.

slides.title: App types in Intune
bullets: Win32 app: your EXE, MSI, or script, packaged as dot-intunewin.
Line-of-business: a single MSI uploaded directly.
Microsoft Store apps and web links.
Microsoft 365 Apps for deploying Office.
slides.narration: Intune supports several app types, one for each kind of source. The workhorse is the Win32 app, which handles custom EXE, MSI, or script installers packaged into a dot-intunewin file. A line-of-business app is just a single MSI you upload directly. There are also Microsoft Store apps, web links that drop a shortcut into the Company Portal, and a guided Microsoft 365 Apps option for deploying Office with the channel and language you choose.

slides.title: Packaging a Win32 app
bullets: Use the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool.
It wraps your source and installer into one dot-intunewin file.
Run IntuneWinAppUtil dot exe with source, setup, and output.
Then set silent install and uninstall commands.
slides.narration: Win32 apps must be wrapped first. The Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool, the executable named Intune-Win-App-Util dot E-X-E, takes your source folder and your setup file and produces one encrypted dot-intunewin package. You point it at the source folder with dash c, the setup file with dash s, and the output folder with dash o. After packaging, you upload it and specify the silent install and uninstall command lines.

slides.title: Detection rules
bullets: Tell Intune whether the app is already installed.
Types: file, registry, MSI product code, or script.
A wrong rule causes false 'Failed' or repeated installs.
Detection drives the 'Installed' status you see.
slides.narration: Every Win32 app needs a detection rule. This is how Intune decides whether the app is already present, so it knows whether to install, skip, or report success. You can detect on a file path, a registry key, an MSI product code, or a custom script. This matters a lot for troubleshooting, because a detection rule that doesn't match what the installer actually drops will show a false failure or cause Intune to keep retrying.

slides.title: Assignment intents
bullets: Required: Intune force-installs automatically.
Available: optional, shows in the Company Portal.
Uninstall: Intune removes the app.
Assign to Microsoft Entra groups.
slides.narration: Adding an app does nothing until you assign it. There are three intents. Required means Intune force-installs the app with no user action. Available means the app is optional and shows up in the Company Portal for the user to install on demand. Uninstall removes the app from the targeted devices. You always assign these to Microsoft Entra groups.

slides.title: User groups vs device groups
bullets: User group: the app follows the person.
Device group: the app stays on the machine.
Available apps usually target users.
Mandatory agents usually target devices.
slides.narration: A key decision is whether to assign to a user group or a device group. Assign to a user group when the app should follow the person, which is typical for Available apps. Assign to a device group when the software must be on that machine no matter who logs in, like a security agent or a kiosk app. Required installs to a device group are how you guarantee something is everywhere.

slides.title: Portal steps
bullets: Go to Apps in the Intune admin center.
Add the app and set install plus detection rules.
Open Assignments and add a group.
Place the group under Required, Available, or Uninstall.
slides.code:
intune.microsoft.com
  > Apps > Windows > + Add
  > Assignments > add group under Required / Available / Uninstall
slides.narration: Here are the portal steps. Sign in to the Intune admin center at intune dot microsoft dot com and open the Apps workload. Click Add, pick your app type, upload the package, and set the install and detection rules. Then open the Assignments tab and add your Entra group under Required, Available, or Uninstall. That's the whole flow from upload to delivery.

slides.title: Troubleshooting and status
bullets: Company Portal shows progress for Available apps.
Device and User install status pages show Installed or Failed.
Check sync, install command, dependencies, detection rule.
Error codes pinpoint the failure.
slides.narration: On the reporting side, the Company Portal shows progress for Available apps, while the admin-side Device install status and User install status pages report Installed, Failed, or Not applicable with an error code. When something fails, confirm the device has synced, verify the silent install command, check for missing dependencies, and re-examine the detection rule. Those four checks resolve most failures.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: App types, packaging, assignment, and status reporting.
Required force-installs; Available is opt-in via Company Portal.
Detection rules decide install state.
Task: package and deploy a free tool in a test tenant.
slides.narration: Let's recap. You now know the Intune app types, how to package a Win32 app with the Content Prep Tool, the difference between Required, Available, and Uninstall, when to target users versus devices, and how detection rules and status pages report results. For your task, package a small free tool like 7-Zip into a dot-intunewin file, upload it as a Win32 app, set a detection rule, assign it as Available to a test user group and confirm it shows in the Company Portal, then add a Required assignment to a device group and verify the install status.
